clue.text: Made-up like Boyd's princess?

explanation.surface: A question whether someone wearing cosmetics resembles a princess in a book by Boyd.
explanation.walkthrough: Martin Boyd, the Australian novelist, wrote the fairy story The Painted Princess (1936).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wearing cosmetics is made-up, and Boyd's princess is named in his title as coloured with paint.

clue.text: Eastern kingdom in fine Palgrave Treasury

indicators.note: in tells us the letters sit inside the run of words fine Palgrave Treasury

explanation.surface: A Himalayan realm tucked into a well-printed copy of Palgrave's Golden Treasury anthology.
explanation.walkthrough: Palgrave's Golden Treasury is a famous Victorian anthology of English verse; the answer runs across 'fiNE PALgrave'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Himalayan state was a monarchy until 2008, a realm lying east of Europe.

clue.text: Who translated Ariosto? Possibly Anon ", right?

indicators.note: possibly suggests the words Anon and right could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Asking whether an anonymous hand produced the English Ariosto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges ANON and RIGHT. Sir John Harington's English Orlando Furioso appeared in 1591.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir John Harington, Elizabeth I's godson, produced the famous English verse rendering of Orlando Furioso.

clue.text: "Out — the web and floated wide" (Tennyson)

parts.note: a line from The Lady of Shalott with one word missing, the verb describing how the web left the loom

explanation.surface: A quotation from Tennyson's poem with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Lady of Shalott the curse falls when 'Out ___ the web and floated wide'; the gap is the past tense of fly.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the verb in Tennyson's line, the past tense meaning soared or sailed off.

clue.text: One of Wilson's nocturnal computers?

parts.note: a portable laptop machine is called by the same name as a jotting pad, the kind of private record a writer called Wilson kept

explanation.surface: A question about a writer named Wilson using computers at night.
explanation.definitionFit: A small laptop machine shares its name with a pad for jottings, the form a writer's private record takes.

clue.text: Persian version of distant Italian agreement

parts.note: distant means far
si is Italian for yes

explanation.surface: A Persian translation of an accord reached in faraway Italy.
explanation.definitionFit: The language of Iran is called by this name, the native word for the Persian tongue.

clue.text: Bacon ascribed it to the queen

definitions.text: Bacon ascribed it to the queen

parts.words: Bacon ascribed it to the queen
parts.note: Francis Bacon wrote a Latin tribute to Elizabeth I praising her good fortune, In felicem memoriam

explanation.surface: The essayist Bacon credits a quality to Queen Elizabeth.
explanation.walkthrough: Bacon's In felicem memoriam Elizabethae celebrates the happy fortune of Elizabeth I's reign.
explanation.definitionFit: Happiness or good fortune is the quality Bacon's Latin title gives the late queen.

clue.text: Snare on Scottish peak for irresponsible father

indicators.note: on means the net is attached after the peak

parts.note: a ben is a Scottish mountain
a snare is a trap, a net

explanation.surface: Trapping something on a Highland summit for a feckless dad.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Bennet of Pride and Prejudice lets his daughters run wild, so is the irresponsible father.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's Mr Bennet is the idle paterfamilias of Pride and Prejudice, who neglects his daughters' welfare.

clue.text: Tense yet apparently confident claim to flawlessness

explanation.walkthrough: Read as two words, the answer says 'I'm perfect', a boast of having no flaws.
explanation.definitionFit: A grammatical tense for unfinished past action has this name, and split it is a boast of being without fault.

clue.text: Gothic novelist as Chaucerian tale-teller

explanation.walkthrough: Clara Reeve (1729-1807) wrote The Old English Baron; in The Canterbury Tales a manorial steward tells a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Clara Reeve wrote The Old English Baron, a Gothic novel, and the Canterbury pilgrim estate manager tells a tale.

clue.text: Attribute of Ripley

parts.note: Patricia Highsmith's anti-hero Tom Ripley is The ... Mr Ripley, so his gift names the attribute

explanation.surface: Asking what quality belongs to someone named Ripley.
explanation.definitionFit: Highsmith's title calls Ripley gifted, and a gift or skill is the attribute named.

clue.text: Cleopatra's was a very Antony

parts.note: Cleopatra says 'O, my ... is a very Antony', meaning her forgetfulness is as bad as her lover

explanation.surface: A remark about Cleopatra's possession being just like Antony.
explanation.walkthrough: In Antony and Cleopatra (I.iii) Cleopatra says 'O, my oblivion is a very Antony, And I am all forgotten.'
explanation.definitionFit: Cleopatra's line names her forgetfulness as the thing that is a very Antony.

clue.text: Old money of the French musical

parts.note: du is French for of the
Cats is the Lloyd Webber musical

explanation.surface: Historic currency of the French musical world.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold coins once used across Europe, the currency Shylock lends.

clue.text: Prolific writer offered transport on property

indicators.note: on in a down clue puts the transport above the property

parts.note: a cart is a means of transport
land is property

explanation.surface: A busy author is offered a vehicle on an estate.
explanation.walkthrough: Barbara Cartland wrote over 700 romantic novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbara Cartland, romance novelist with over 700 books, was famously productive.

clue.text: Mary Braddon's struggle

parts.note: M. E. Braddon, author of Lady Audley's Secret, wrote a 1903 novel titled with a word for a fight

explanation.surface: The battle of the Victorian novelist Mary Braddon.
explanation.definitionFit: A fight or clash is a struggle, and Braddon used the word as a novel title.

clue.text: Shakespearean king, later seen as wolfish duke

explanation.walkthrough: In The Duchess of Malfi, written after Shakespeare's play, Duke Ferdinand goes mad and believes he is a wolf.
explanation.definitionFit: Love's Labour's Lost has a king of Navarre so named, and Webster's Duchess of Malfi has a duke with lycanthropy.

clue.text: There was room for him in Baldwin's work

definitions.text: There was room for him in Baldwin's work

parts.words: There was room for him in Baldwin's work
parts.note: James Baldwin's novel is named after the room of an Italian character

explanation.surface: Someone found space for a person in Baldwin's writing.
explanation.walkthrough: James Baldwin's 1956 novel is Giovanni's Room.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian barman of Baldwin's novel gives his name to its title, so the room is his.

clue.text: Sort of medicine prescribed for Corn well protagonist

explanation.walkthrough: Patricia Cornwell's heroine Kay Scarpetta is a medical examiner; 'Corn well' is the newspaper's split of Cornwell.
explanation.definitionFit: The medicine of legal evidence has this adjective, and Patricia Cornwell's Kay Scarpetta is a pathologist in that line.

clue.text: Sort of king knowing a few angles, having suffered a dolorous stroke?

definitions.text: Sort of king knowing a few angles, having suffered a dolorous stroke?

parts.words: Sort of king knowing a few angles, having suffered a dolorous stroke?
parts.note: the wounded keeper of the Grail in Arthurian legend, struck by the Dolorous Stroke, passes time by angling

explanation.surface: A king who knows some geometry and has had an unfortunate stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: In Arthurian legend the Grail king was maimed by the Dolorous Stroke and spends his days angling; 'angles' puns on fishing.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler is so called, and the maimed Grail guardian is that sort of king.

clue.text: Heart of Midlothian character seen in depths of lethargy, let down by friends

indicators.note: seen in depths of signals letters lying buried inside the words lethargy, let

explanation.surface: A character from Scott's novel spotted deep in lethargy, disappointed by friends.
explanation.walkthrough: The Heart of Midlothian is Walter Scott's novel, in which the Duke of Argyle wins Jeanie Deans her sister's pardon; the answer spans 'lethARGY LEt'. 'Heart' is part of the title, not a centre indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's Duke of Argyle is the nobleman who helps Jeanie Deans in the novel.

clue.text: This footman held Prufrock's coat

parts.note: in T. S. Eliot's poem Prufrock sees death as an everlasting footman holding his coat and snickering

explanation.surface: A servant took the coat of someone called Prufrock.
explanation.walkthrough: Eliot's line is 'I have seen the eternal Footman hold my coat, and snicker'.
explanation.definitionFit: Eliot's footman is everlasting, death personified, and the clue asks for his epithet.

clue.text: Malvolio was sick of it

parts.note: in Twelfth Night Olivia tells Malvolio that he is sick of excessive regard for himself

explanation.surface: Someone named Malvolio had had enough of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Olivia in Twelfth Night (I.v): 'O, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio.' 'Sick of' means ill with, not tired of.
explanation.definitionFit: Olivia diagnoses Malvolio's vanity as a sickness, an excess of narcissism.

clue.text: French and English articles inducing forgetfulness ()

parts.note: le is a French article, the
the is the English definite article

explanation.surface: Grammatical articles in two languages that make you forget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French and English articles' gives one article from each language.
explanation.definitionFit: The river of the underworld whose water makes the dead forget is the source of forgetfulness.

clue.text: Bacon's jester

parts.note: Bacon's essay Of Truth opens 'What is truth? said jesting ...'

explanation.surface: A court fool belonging to Bacon.
explanation.walkthrough: Bacon's essay Of Truth opens: 'What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.'
explanation.definitionFit: Bacon's essay calls the Roman governor who tried Jesus jesting, making him a jester.

clue.text: Excuse for starting a long, interesting book immediately

indicators.note: for starting asks for the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A pretext for beginning a long, gripping book right away.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea that one was elsewhere is the classic excuse.

clue.text: Wilder portrayal of sweet character

explanation.surface: A wilder depiction of a sweet person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilder' is Billy Wilder, director of Irma la Douce (1963); douce is French for sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: The Parisian heroine of Wilder's film is called the sweet one in her title.

clue.text: English navy way of surrealist

explanation.surface: The English navy's approach to a surrealist.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Ernst was a German surrealist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Max Ernst, Dada and surrealist painter, is an example of a surrealist.

clue.text: An account of Gertrude Stein

parts.note: Gertrude Stein gave a set of lectures in 1935 published under a title meaning storytelling

explanation.surface: A description of the writer Gertrude Stein.
explanation.walkthrough: Stein's 1935 Chicago lectures were published as Narration.

a hill is a rise
